comment.value: This paper introduces Gradual Binary Search and Hadamard-based dimension expansion for activation quantization in LLMs, showing promising empirical improvements at 3–4 bits. However, reviewers found the theoretical contributions weak and narrowly scoped, with proofs unconvincing and lacking validation on real model activations. The empirical evaluation, while extensive in benchmarks, omits critical ablations (e.g., non-gradual or alternative heuristics), relies on heavy calibration (up to 4 days per model), and demonstrates no real-world hardware benefits. Despite interesting ideas, the combination of limited theory, incomplete validation, and impractical computational demands leads to the conclusion that the paper does not meet the NeurIPS acceptance bar. All reviewers leaned toward rejection.

Thank you for the detailed rebuttal. My post-rebuttal comments are below.

**[Q1] Question regarding dimension expansion**. I appreciate the clarification and the concrete example showing that the proposed dimension-expansion trick can indeed extend QuaRot to additional models.

**[Q2] Concern regarding the Benefit of Gradual Binary Search (GBS).** While GBS yields a larger boost in the 3-bit setting, the 3-bit models still lag their full-precision baselines by a substantial margin. In 4-bit quantization, the benefit appears to shrink as stronger rotation schemes are adopted: Table 1 reports a 4.6-point gain when GBS is added to vanilla QuaRot, but only a 0.5-point gain when combined with SpinQuant. This limited incremental value tempers the practical appeal of GBS.

**[Q3] Concern on the compute cost of GBS**. The additional ablation is helpful. I encourage the authors to integrate these results into the main paper so that readers can better judge the accuracy–cost trade-off.

The rebuttal resolves my concerns in Q1 and Q3, so I have raised my score from 2 to 3. Nonetheless, several limitations prevent a higher rating: (i) the non-trivial accuracy gap at 3 bits and diminishing returns at 4 bits, and (ii) the fact that dimension expansion is needed only for QuaRot’s fixed Hadamard rotations. Because more advanced learned-rotation methods such as SpinQuant impose no dimensional constraints, the contribution of the proposed techniques remains narrow.

We thank the reviewer for their time and comments. We hope to have addressed their remaining concerns below.

$\textbf{Q1.}$ Can the author provide the efficiency evaluations of non-power-of-2 Hadamard Transforms to their power-of-2 2 counterparts using dimension increasing? 

$\textbf{A1.}$ First we want to answer your concerns about the 1536 dimension needing dimension expansion to make QuaRot work. It was a mistake and we apologize for this confusion. As you well explained we can decompose it with 1536 = 12*128 which is a composition of a power of 2 matrix and a know Hadamard dimension. But dimension  expansion is still necessary for the MLP which is in dimension 18944 which can be decomposed as 18944 = 128x148 but 148 is not a known dimension for an Hadamard matrix even for the Paley algorithm introduced in the paper. So we need to expand these projections (Gate and Up) to reach 18976 = 8x2372 where 2372 validates the conditions of the Paley algorithm and it is also a decomposition that can be used efficiently by the Group Local Rotation of QuaRot. We could improve this method by searching for an expanding dimension which reaches a decomposition that leads to a lower-dimensional decomposition, thereby reducing 2372, which can be very large to store in memory.
In this case, the fast-hadamard-transform library is used with the decomposition 18976 = 8x2372 with 8 a power of 2

$\textbf{Q2.}$  DuQuant [1] is cited in the paper; could the proposed GBS still yield benefits on the advanced rotation matrices?

$\textbf{A2.}$ We haven't tested GBS on that particular method but there is no reason it wouldn't work. Our results on 3 different methods : QuaRot, SpinQuant and DFRot show the versatility of GBS which outperform all these methods in 4 and 3 bits almost all the time. Although GBS remains below baseline accuracy on benchmarks at 3-bit precision, it significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods. This is the main contribution of our paper: 3-bit quantization of both weights and activations is now a realistic possibility.

$\textbf{Weakness 3.}$ The authors report running GBS on one A100 for four days (~96 GPU-hours) using only 10 % of WikiText-2 for the largest models. This cost is far above that of the “fast PTQ” baselines and can even exceed the 41 A100 hours budget for running QAT reported in EfficientQAT [1].

$\textbf{A3.}$
As pointed out by other reviewers our method's computation's cost is high. We conducted an ablation study on 2 parameters that can influence the computation time: $\alpha$ the size of the dataset and max_iter the maximum number iterations allowed for the bianry search. Here is a summary of our results:

| Model | Bit | α (%) | max_iter | time(h) | PPL |
|-------|-----|-------|----------|---------|-----|
| Llama2-7b | 4 | 10 | 10 | 50| 6.04 |
| | | | 8 | 31.9 | 6.07 |
| | | | 7 | 28.6 | 6.08 |
| | | | 6 | 24.7 | 6.08 |
| | | | 5 | 21.02 | 6.08 |
| | | | 4 | 17.42 | 6.09 |
| | | | 3 | 14.07 | 6.37 |
| | | 5 | 5 | 10.89 | 6.11 |
| | 3| 10 | 10 | 50| 9.18 |
| | | | 5| 21| 10.39 |
| | | 5| 5| 10| 15.72 |
| Llama3-8b | 4 | 10 | 10 | 80 | 7.4 |
|  |  | | 5| 19.5| 7.53 |
|  |  | 5| 5| 10.02| 7.56 |
|  |3 |10 | 10| 80| 12.62 |
|  | |10 | 5| 19.44| 15.65 |
|  |  | 5| 5| 10.02| 15.72 |

In this table we can clearly see we can improve the computation time with these 2 paramters. On a Llama2-7B we can reduce to 10h without a significant drop of perplexity. In 3 bits the model is more sensitive and we can see a drop but still remaining well better than previous state of the art methods. We can also drastically reduce the computation time for Llama3-8B with a small PPL increase (+0.13 in best case in 4 bits). While the results aren't yet optimal, they clearly demonstrate that more effective clipping ratio optimization is crucial for substantial performance gains.

We thank the reviewer for their time and comments. We hope to have addressed their remaining concerns below.

$\textbf{Q1.}$ and $\textbf{Q2.}$ How does the method perform on extremely large models (70B+ parameters)? The current experiments are limited to models up to 8B parameters. Does the effectiveness of GBS scale to larger models where outlier patterns might be different?  What is the relationship between the number of GBS iterations and final performance? Is there a point of diminishing returns, and how can practitioners determine the optimal number of iterations for their specific use case?

$\textbf{A1.}$ and $\textbf{A2.}$ We couldn't actually apply our method on bigger models like 70B parameters because we don't have enough GPUs to perform inference and to just store the model. As pointed above our method GBS is very compute demanding so we conducted several experiments to sudy the impact of the size of the dataset ($\alpha$) and the maximum number of iterations (max_iter) for the binary search and here are our results :

| Model | Bit | α (%) | max_iter | time(h) | PPL |
|-------|-----|-------|----------|---------|-----|
| Llama2-7b | 4 | 10 | 10 | 50| 6.04 |
| | | | 8 | 31.9 | 6.07 |
| | | | 7 | 28.6 | 6.08 |
| | | | 6 | 24.7 | 6.08 |
| | | | 5 | 21.02 | 6.08 |
| | | | 4 | 17.42 | 6.09 |
| | | | 3 | 14.07 | 6.37 |
| | | 5 | 5 | 10.89 | 6.11 |
| | 3| 10 | 10 | 50| 9.18 |
| | | | 5| 21| 10.39 |
| | | 5| 5| 10| 15.72 |
| Llama3-8b | 4 | 10 | 10 | 80 | 7.4 |
|  |  | | 5| 19.5| 7.53 |
|  |  | 5| 5| 10.02| 7.56 |
|  |3 |10 | 10| 80| 12.62 |
|  | |10 | 5| 19.44| 15.65 |
|  |  | 5| 5| 10.02| 15.72 |

We tested on 2 models how these 2 parameters impact the computation time and we can see that it can be reduced to 10h for Llama2-7B without hurting performances. We also notice this model is more sensitive to $\alpha$ than max_iter but it seems to be the opposite for Llama3-8B. 3 bits is also more challenging and performances face a bigger drop when we change the computation demand.
We tested different values for max_iter and we can see that 3 is a turning point where GBS start to not perform well with a drop of 0.3 of PPL in 4 bits but we think this threshold can be different for other models.
Despite their limitations, these results clearly underscore the importance of refining the clipping ratio to unlock stronger performance gains

$\textbf{Q3.}$ How does GBS interact with other quantization techniques? Can it be combined with methods like group-wise quantization or mixed-precision approaches to achieve even better results?

$\textbf{A3.}$ Yes GBS is very general and only needs to change the clipping ratio and compute perplexity to be used which makes it work with all other types of quantization techniques like mix-precision or group-wise quantization. Also we didn't compare our method GBS with GPTQ or AWQ which are weights only quantization because we perform weight and activation quantization 

$\textbf{Q4.}$ What is the impact on inference latency? While the paper shows perplexity improvements, how does the additional reshaping affect actual inference speed on various hardware platforms?

$\textbf{A4.}$ There are 2 main objectives of dimension expansion: make rotation matices work with non-power of 2 dimensions and improve performances. In the first case it doesn't increase the computation stress, for example in the case of Qwen2.5-7B we only need to increase up to 32 dimensions the MLP which doesn't affect inference time in a significant amount.
In the case we want to improve precision and performances  to reach the baseline like in Figure 2, it also increases the number of operations done at inference because we add a lot of dimensions. If we use BitOps as a metric to quantify computational demand, increasing by $d$ dimensions increases the number of BitOps by $m(2dn + d^2)pb^2$ with $n$ and $p$ the matrix dimensions, $m$ the input dimension and $b$ the bitwidth

$\textbf{Q5.}$ Can the binary search bounds be learned or adapted based on model characteristics? The current approach seems to use fixed search bounds, but could these be optimized per layer or model type?

$\textbf{A5.}$ The search is carried out across the entire space, taking the full minimum and maximum bounds, but the nature of the binary algorithm allows for immediately reducing this range by converging toward the most optimal part of the search space. So it is kind of learnt for every model and every layer implicitly.

$\textbf{Q6.}$ How robust is the method to different types of outliers? Are there specific activation patterns or outlier distributions where GBS might be less effective?

$\textbf{A6.}$ We didn't notice a particular type of outlier with which GBS struggles to converge or improve performance, in all the experiments we did on QuaRot, SpinQuant, DFRot, in 4 bits or 3 bits GBS successfully improved PPL and accuracy on common benchmarks

We thank the reviewer for their time and comments. We hope to have addressed their remaining concerns below.

$\textbf{Q1.}$The fast Hadamard transform algorithm is only applicable to power-of-two dimensions. Does your method only use non-power-of-two Hadamard where it can be merged into the weight matrix? Notice that, based on Quarot, not all of them can be merged.

$\textbf{A1.}$ It is only the case for Qwen2.5 7B Instruct where we also need to expand the MLP part of the model which projects our tokens in a 18944 dimensions space which can be decomposed as 18944 = 128x148 but 148 is not a know dimension for an Hadamard matrix even for the Paley algorithm introduced in the paper. So we need to expand this projections (Gate and Up) to reach 18976 = 8x2372 where 2372 validates the condition of the Paley algorithm and it is also a decomposition that can be used efficiently by the Group Local Rotation of QuaRot. We could improve this method by expanding by more dimensions to reach a decomposition with lower dimensions and reduce 2372 which can be really big to keep in memory.

$\textbf{Q2.}$ How does your results change if you use Group Local Rotation (e.g., Hadamard in three groups of 512 for dimension 1536)? I think having this result strengthens your paper.

$\textbf{A2.}$ Group Local Rotation are still used in our process, but you are right there is a mistake in our paper 1536 can actually work without expanding dimensions and only the MLP needs to be expanded as explained above, we apologize for this confusion and we will correct it in the paper.

$\textbf{Q3.}$ Do your theoretical results extend to the case where multiple outliers exist in the input matrix, as it’s usually the case in activation matrices?

$\textbf{A3.}$ Yes it should extends to multiple outliers. We conducted some experiments to see how it evolves with the dimension and the number of outliers and it looks like the reduction factor between Random Orthogonal and Hadamard  is something like
$R(n, k) =\frac{\max_i |(Qx)_i|}{\max_i |(Hx)_i|} \approx A \cdot \frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{k}}$
With $n$ the number of dimensions and $k$ the number of outliers, the proof is still in progress but we have some starting points. These results show that the maximum obtained after applying a Random Rotation Matrix $Q$ and a Hadamard matrix $H$ is bigger for $Q$ than $H$ even for multiple outliers and the difference increase with dimension. We still need to refine the proof so if you have any question let us know.

$\textbf{Q4.}$ Can you elaborate on why Theorem 3.2 shows Hadamard optimality?

$\textbf{A4.}$ First, as you noticed we used the same $\epsilon$ for the definition of the vector with an outlier and the application of  Talagrand’s inequality which is in fact not the same $\epsilon$ and we apologize for this mistake which will be corrected. 

About the optimality, with our hypothesis of an outlier $c$ inside a vector with small values we use $\max_i|(Hx)_i| = c \cdot \max_k |H_k|$ so we only need to compute the maximum of the Hadamard matrix to know its effect on the vector.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for their time and comments. We hope to have addressed their remaining concerns below.

$\textbf{Q1}$. The theoretic result that Hadamard rotation reduces outliers more than a random rotation needs experimental corroboration.

$\textbf{A1}$. Can you be more precise on what you actually want to be tested differently from the experimental verification in Appendix A.1.2 ? In this appendix we experimentally verifiy the theorem 3.1 by testing the effect of a Hadamard matrix on an Gaussian distributed matrix with an outlier of 200 and compare it with a randomly drawn rotation matrix and clearly see that the theoretical model perfectly follows the experimental one for both cases showing the effectiveness of a Hadamard matrix.

$\textbf{Q2.}$ The claim of the effectiveness of clipping ratio as a heuristic lacks adequate experimental support.

$\textbf{A2.}$ To perform GBS we chose to use the perplexity as an heuristic to optimize the clipping ratio of every layers and every projections for 2 main reasons:

       - Quantization error which is often used to drive this type of optimization isn't always correlated with good application performances and a low quantization error doesn't imply better performance espacially at very low precision
       - Perplexity is a better heuristic because it is fast to compute and represents better performances, we tried to show this experimentally in appendix D

Can you be more precise on what kind of experiments you would like too see ?

$\textbf{Q3.}$The effectiveness of the gradual binary search algorithm lack adequate ablation study: what if it was non-gradual, or reverse-gradual, what about other optimization than binary search?

$\textbf{A3.}$
We didn't try a non gradual optimzation because it is harder to implement an algorithm that would directly find the best configuration for every parameter at once but also the gradual method helps correct errors caused by successive quantization wich make it easier to implement with good results.

For the reverse gradual we tried it a few months ago by starting by the last layer and gradually quantizatizing and optimizing the model until reaching the first layer but we didn't notice any benefits from it so we didn't include it. If necessary we can add it to the appendix.

The reason we opted for a binary search is to enable faster and more efficient convergence toward an appropriate clipping ratio, rather than relying on a uniform grid whose number of units must be predefined. Experimental results show that below a certain clipping ratio threshold, performance drops drastically, making it unnecessary to test lower values. This threshold can vary significantly depending on the layer being optimized, making it difficult to define a global threshold. Binary search addresses this issue by avoiding exploration in irrelevant regions and quickly converging toward a clipping ratio that improves performance. So we didn't try a grid search for example because it didn't seem necessary compared to the binary search.

$\textbf{Q4.}$ In reality, given a particular hardware set up, does the proposed method lead to Pareto-optimal models for inference, with varied models, PTQ methods and numerical precisions? Given that now expansion dimension is another free parameter, the search space is larger.

$\textbf{A4.}$ Our method does not alter the way the computation is performed; it only optimizes the clipping ratio that defines the quantization bounds. As for the dimensional expansion, it is a parameter to be chosen beforehand, depending on the desired performance gain relative to the acceptable computational overhead. This is a trade-off specific to the user's needs.

summary.value: In this paper, the authors first theoretically show that Hadamard-based rotations are more effective than random rotations on the unit sphere for mitigating outliers. Then, they take advantage of the Paley algorithm, a method to generate Hadamard matrices for any dimension 4k where 4k-1 is a prime number. Additionally, they introduce (a) dimension expansion before rotation, and show that expanding dimensions before rotation can allow for better outlier mitigation while increasing computational cost, and (b) Gradual Binary Search (GBS) to gradually find optimal clipping ratio for model layers while using final perplexity of the model as metric. Experiments show that combining existing methods such as Quarot with GBS improves their results significantly, and dimension expansion can further improve the results at the cost of compute.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. Quantizing gradually with PPL as the metric seems to be effective.
2. The paper is well-written.
3. The experiments are extensive with strong results.
4. Paley’s algorithms extend the dimension for which we have Hadamard matrices, allowing us to better control the dimension expansion (padding).

Weaknesses (see the Questions section below):
1. I find the theoretical results on Hadamard optimality unconvincing: (a) only a special case is considered, where the input vector has a single outlier, (b) theorem statements/proofs are informal, although they seem correct: epsilons ignored in the proof of Lemma 3.1, and Lemma 3.2 holds with high probability, which is not mentioned in the main text. (c) It’s not clear why Theorem 3.2 means Hadamard is optimal, when it’s just bounding the maximum element of the rotation itself, and not the rotated input vector.
2. You mention Group-Local Rotation, where power-of-two Hadamards are applied to sub-matrices. For example, note that in case of Qwen 2.5 1.5B, the dimension 1536 = 512 * 3. It’s not clear how the method performs under such faster transforms.
3. I think GBS with perplexity as the metric is too computationally expensive, already taking around 4 days for an 8B model.

questions.value:
1. The fast Hadamard transform algorithm is only applicable to power-of-two dimensions. Does your method only use non-power-of-two Hadamard where it can be merged into the weight matrix? Notice that, based on Quarot, not all of them can be merged.
2. How does your results change if you use Group Local Rotation (e.g., Hadamard in three groups of 512 for dimension 1536)? I think having this result strengthens your paper.
3. Do your theoretical results extend to the case where multiple outliers exist in the input matrix, as it’s usually the case in activation matrices?
4. Can you elaborate on why Theorem 3.2 shows Hadamard optimality?
5. As you mentioned, 10% of wikitext seems a lot compared to other baselines. I think a study on the size of calibration data vs accuracy is crucial, as the method is not applicable to larger models in this state.

While GBS and dimension expansion are interesting and offer strong results, I still have two main concerns regarding this paper: (1) I am not convinced by the theoretical results regarding Hadamard optimality, and (2) the method is not applicable to larger models in the current state due to very high computational cost. I am open to increasing my score if the authors can address my concerns, especially 3, 4, and 5.

summary.value: The paper proposes a post-training weight and activation quantization framework for LLM. It adopted Hadamard rotation for eliminating outliers in activation with a Gradual Binary Search (GBS) algorithm that finds a proper clipping ratio for each projection by minimizing perplexity during successive quantization steps. The authors also add a padding-based “dimension expansion” trick to get rid of the dimensional restriction to generalize the applicability of Hadamard rotation.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
## Strengths
1. **Providing theoretical backing for using Hadamard rotations.**
2. **Broad evaluation across model families**  Experiments span Mistral, Llama-2, Llama-3, and Qwen.

## Weaknesses
1. **Potentially Incorrect Power-of-2 Limitation and Marginal Benefit from Dimension Expansion**
    + To the best of my understanding, Quarot does not have a strict limitation on the power of 2 Hadamard transforms (L189\~L190). In Quip#, the work that inspired QuaRot, the authors state that non-power-of-2 Hadamard transforms can be obtained via a Kronecker product between a non-power-of-2 Hadamard matrix and a power-of-2 Hadamard matrix. For example, the 1536] dim case mentioned in the paper (L246~L247) can be realized as  $H_{1536} = H_{12} \otimes H_{128}$. 

    + The official QuaRot implementation [3] already uses this trick to support the 1536-dim Hadamard transform. 

   + More generally, if a target dimension can be decomposed into a power-of-two factor and another factor for which a Hadamard matrix exists, then a Hadamard transform of that dimension should, in principle, be supported. Considering the existence of a wide variety of Hadamard matrices with different dimensions [4], the proposed  _Increasing Dimension_ techniques seem to offer marginal benefit. 

2. **Limited Benefit of Gradual Binary Search (GBS) when Enhanced Rotation Matrices are Adopted**
    + GBS appears to deliver a large gain (~3 percentage-point average accuracy in Table 1). However, when paired with stronger rotation matrices such as the learned rotations in SpinQuant presented in Table 3, the improvement is marginal (< 1 in average accuracy at the W4A4KV4 setting).
    + Although the authors show W3A3 results where GBS provides noticeable benefits, the final accuracy still lags the full-precision model by roughly 30 pp on Llama-3-8B, raising concerns about practical value.

3. **High Computational Cost of GBS**
    + The authors report running GBS on one A100 for four days (~96 GPU-hours) using only 10 % of WikiText-2 for the largest models. This cost is far above that of the “fast PTQ” baselines and can even exceed the 41 A100 hours budget for running QAT reported in EfficientQAT [1]. 

[1] EfficientQAT: Efficient Quantization-Aware Training for Large Language Models

[2] SpinQuant: LLM quantization with learned rotations

[3] https://github.com/spcl/QuaRot/blob/main/fake_quant/hadamard_utils.py#L92

[4] http://neilsloane.com/hadamard/

final_justification.value:
I have raised my score from 2 → 3 because the rebuttal satisfactorily addressed my technical concerns in Q1 and Q3. Two practical-impact limitations, however, still keep the work below the acceptance bar:

**Accuracy gap:**
At 3-bit, the models remain notably below full precision, and at 4-bit, the gains are only modest, especially when stronger rotation (such as SpinQuant) methods are used.

**Narrow applicability:**
Dimension expansion is needed only for QuaRot’s fixed Hadamard rotations. For modern learned-rotation approaches, such as SpinQuant, face no dimensional constraints, which limits the broader relevance of the proposed technique.

Given these constraints, I recommend a weak reject (score = 3).

summary.value: This paper introduces Gradual Binary Search (GBS), a novel approach to mitigate outlier issues in quantized Large Language Models (LLMs) by progressively redistributing activation outliers across multiple dimensions through iterative tensor reshaping and rotation. The method builds upon existing rotation-based quantization techniques like QuaRot, addressing the fundamental challenge that outliers tend to concentrate in specific channels after rotation, which degrades quantization performance. GBS employs a binary search strategy to identify optimal reshaping factors that minimize the infinity norm of rotated tensors, effectively spreading outliers more evenly across dimensions. Experimental results on various LLMs including Llama2, Llama3, and Qwen2.5 models demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline QuaRot methods across multiple benchmarks, with the approach showing particular effectiveness for smaller models where outlier concentration poses more significant challenges.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths**

1. Novel theoretical framework for outlier redistribution: The paper presents a mathematically grounded approach to address outlier concentration through dimensional expansion and iterative refinement. The binary search mechanism for finding optimal reshaping factors provides a principled way to minimize the infinity norm of rotated tensors, which directly correlates with quantization error reduction.

2. Consistent empirical improvements across diverse models: The experimental results demonstrate that GBS consistently improves upon QuaRot baselines across different model architectures and sizes. For instance, on Llama3 8B, GBS improves the average score from 59.97 to 65.71, showing substantial gains particularly on tasks like PIQA (57.05 to 63.73) and ARC-e (42.06 to 45.9).

3. Scalability to different model sizes: The method shows effectiveness across various model scales, from Qwen2.5 1.5B to Llama3 8B, with particularly notable improvements for smaller models where outlier issues are more pronounced. This suggests the approach is generally applicable rather than tailored to specific architectures.

4. Computational efficiency: By using binary search to find optimal parameters, the method appears to be computationally tractable compared to exhaustive search approaches, making it practical for real-world deployment scenarios.

**Weaknesses**

1. Limited discussion of computational overhead: While the paper mentions using binary search for efficiency, it lacks detailed analysis of the actual computational cost and memory overhead introduced by the iterative reshaping process. The time complexity and memory requirements during the GBS optimization phase should be quantified and compared to baseline methods.

2. Incomplete baseline comparisons: The paper primarily compares against QuaRot and its variants but lacks comprehensive comparison with other recent quantization methods. Notable omissions include:

   -GPTQ (Generative Pre-trained Transformer Quantization)

    -AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization)

    -GGUF (GPT-Generated Unified Format) quantization methods

    -Recent methods like SpQR (Sparse-Quantized Representation) and QuIP (Quantization with Incoherence Processing)

3. Missing recent relevant literature: The paper should incorporate more recent developments in LLM quantization, particularly:

    -"OmniQuant: Omnidirectionally Calibrated Quantization for Large Language Models" (2024)

    -"QLLM: Accurate and Efficient Low-Bitwidth Quantization for Large Language Models" (2024)

    -"BitNet: Scaling 1-bit Transformers for Large Language Models" (2024)

    -"SqueezeLLM: Dense-and-Sparse Quantization" (2024)

    -"AffineQuant: Affine Transformation Quantization for Large Language Models" (2024)

4. Limited analysis of failure cases: The results show that Qwen2.5 models with QuaRot baseline failed (indicated by dashes in the table), but there's insufficient discussion about why these failures occurred and how GBS specifically addresses these failure modes.

5. Lack of bit-width exploration: The paper appears to focus on a specific quantization bit-width but doesn't explore how the method performs across different quantization levels (e.g., 2-bit, 3-bit, 4-bit, 8-bit), which is crucial for understanding the method's generalizability.

questions.value:
1. How does the method perform on extremely large models (70B+ parameters)? The current experiments are limited to models up to 8B parameters. Does the effectiveness of GBS scale to larger models where outlier patterns might be different?

2. What is the relationship between the number of GBS iterations and final performance? Is there a point of diminishing returns, and how can practitioners determine the optimal number of iterations for their specific use case?

3. How does GBS interact with other quantization techniques? Can it be combined with methods like group-wise quantization or mixed-precision approaches to achieve even better results?

4. What is the impact on inference latency? While the paper shows perplexity improvements, how does the additional reshaping affect actual inference speed on various hardware platforms?

5. Can the binary search bounds be learned or adapted based on model characteristics? The current approach seems to use fixed search bounds, but could these be optimized per layer or model type?

6. How robust is the method to different types of outliers? Are there specific activation patterns or outlier distributions where GBS might be less effective?

title.value: Gradual Binary Search and Dimension Expansion : A general method for activation quantization in LLMs

abstract.value: Large language models (LLMs) have become pivotal in artificial intelligence, demonstrating strong capabilities in reasoning, understanding, and generating data. However, their deployment on edge devices is hindered by their substantial size, often reaching several billion parameters. Quantization is a widely used method to reduce memory usage and inference time, however LLMs present unique challenges due to the prevalence of outliers in their activations. In this work, we leverage the theoretical advantages of Hadamard matrices over random rotation matrices to push the boundaries of quantization in LLMs. We demonstrate that Hadamard matrices are more effective in reducing outliers, which are a significant obstacle in achieving low-bit quantization. Our method based on a gradual binary search enables 3-bit quantization for weights, activations, and key-value (KV) caches, resulting in a 40% increase in accuracy on common benchmarks compared to SoTA methods. We extend the use of rotation matrices to support non-power-of-2 embedding dimensions, similar to the Qwen architecture, by employing the Paley's algorithm. Our experimental results on multiple models family like Mistral, LLaMA, and Qwen demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming existing methods and enabling practical 3-bit quantization.
